Everythingin orbit

The public satellite catalog, October 1957 to September 2026By Alejandro Pacheco

The U.S. Space Force keeps a catalog of every object it tracks in orbit around Earth, and CelesTrak publishes it as a single public file. It lists 70,745 objects launched since Sputnik: 27,788 payloads, 6,902 spent rocket bodies, 35,889 pieces of debris and 166 objects nobody has identified, and about half of them have since fallen back into the atmosphere. The report below follows how the catalog grew, who owns the objects and where they sit. Two thirds of all payloads ever launched went up after 2019, most of them Starlink satellites, and in June 2024 payloads in orbit outnumbered debris for the first time since 1961. They have stayed ahead since October 2024.

Two thirds of all payloads ever launched went up after 2019

From 1957 through 2019 the world launched 8,869 payloads, rarely more than a few hundred in a year. In 2020 the count jumped to 1,257, and it kept rising, to 4,506 in 2025 and 3,226 in the first nine months of 2026. Of the 27,788 payloads in the catalog, 18,919 (68.1%) were launched in 2020 or later.

Scrolling on runs the catalog back to October 1957 and then forward again. Each point on the globe is one tracked object, drawn on its cataloged orbit, appearing when it entered the catalog and sinking out of sight when it reentered.

Starlink satellites are 65% of the payloads working today

SpaceX has launched 12,863 Starlink satellites since May 2019. Of these, 11,107 are listed as active, which is 64.9% of the 17,112 active payloads in the catalog, and 1,754 have already reentered. Starlink accounts for 66.3% of all payloads launched from 2019 on.

Because Starlink is a U.S. company, the United States now owns 12,924 of the active payloads, against 1,548 for China, 698 for the United Kingdom (mostly the OneWeb constellation) and 385 for Russia.

Payloads have outnumbered debris in orbit since October 2024

For most of the space age, fragments were the largest group of objects in orbit. Tracked debris in Earth orbit peaked at 14,898 pieces on 1 February 2022, just after the Cosmos 1408 test, and has since fallen to 12,521, because more low fragments reentered than new ones were cataloged. Over the same years the number of payloads in orbit went from 5,265 at the start of 2020 to 19,956 today.

In June 2024 payloads in orbit outnumbered debris for the first time since mid-1961. Debris was briefly ahead again in September, and payloads have stayed ahead since October 2024. Spent rocket bodies grew slowly throughout and stand at 2,299.

Ten launches produced a third of all cataloged debris

The catalog lists 35,889 debris pieces that trace back to 3,117 launches, but 11,454 of them (31.9%) come from only ten. The largest source is the Chinese weather satellite Fengyun 1C, destroyed in a 2007 missile test, with 3,534 pieces. Next are Cosmos 1408, destroyed in a 2021 Russian missile test (1,806 pieces), and the two satellites in the 2009 collision, Cosmos 2251 and Iridium 33 (1,716 and 656 pieces). Two Long March 6A upper stages that broke apart shortly after launch in 2022 and 2024 added 800 and 705 more.

How long the pieces stay up depends on their altitude. Cosmos 1408 was in a low orbit, and all but 4 of its pieces have reentered, while 65.5% of the Fengyun 1C pieces and 77% and 82% of the two Long March 6A clouds, which orbit near 750 km, are still up.

U.S. payloads went from 13.9% of payloads launched in the 1980s to 78.5% in the 2020s

In the 1970s and 1980s the Soviet Union launched 73% to 78% of all payloads. Its successor's share fell to 9.5% in the 2010s and 1.9% so far in the 2020s. The U.S. share rose from 13.9% in the 1980s to 78.5% in the 2020s, and 12,743 of the 14,852 U.S. payloads of the 2020s are Starlink satellites.

Leaving Starlink out, the 2020s split into roughly three parts: 34.1% United States, 25.2% China and 34.8% everyone else, with Russia at 5.8%. The number of different owners putting up payloads grew from 10 in the 1960s to 101 in the 2010s.

84% of the objects in orbit are below 2,000 km, in two crowded bands

Of the 34,500 objects in Earth orbit with a known orbit, 28,996 (84.0%) circle below 2,000 km. The busiest band is 450 to 500 km, with 9,963 objects, of which 9,198 are Starlink satellites. A second band, from 700 to 900 km, holds 5,652 objects, and 4,665 of them are debris; this is where the Fengyun 1C test and the 2009 collision took place.

Farther out, 1,755 objects have a perigee of 35,000 km or more. Of the 1,741 among them on near-circular orbits, 1,512 have a mean altitude within 500 km of the geosynchronous altitude of 35,786 km, the ring drawn around the globe. At that altitude an orbit takes one day, so a satellite over the equator stays above the same point on the ground. Here the globe draws heights on a square-root scale, so the low shells separate.

Three orbital tilts hold almost half of everything in orbit

Inclination is the angle between an orbit and the equator. 5,167 objects fly between 53 and 54 degrees and 3,583 between 43 and 44 degrees, and nearly all of them are Starlink satellites. The band from 97 to 99 degrees holds 7,447 more. At those tilts an orbit is sun-synchronous: it passes over each place at the same local time every day, which Earth-imaging and weather satellites rely on.

Together the three bands hold 16,197 objects, 47% of everything in Earth orbit with a known tilt. The globe here is seen from above the North Pole, and the three bands are the ones drawn in color.

Below 600 km objects are new; higher up, many are decades old

Below 600 km, air drag brings an object down within a few years once it stops raising its orbit, so what is there is new: the median object between 400 and 500 km entered the catalog 1.9 years ago. Higher up, the air is too thin to clear anything out. The median object between 700 and 900 km has been in the catalog for about 17 years, and between 1,500 and 2,000 km for 39 years. The band from 1,000 to 1,200 km is younger (median 9.6 years) because 708 of its 2,039 objects belong to the OneWeb, Qianfan and Hulianwang constellations, launched from 2019 on; without them its median is 20.4 years.

The oldest object still in orbit is Vanguard 1, a U.S. satellite launched in March 1958, on an orbit of 652 by 3,818 km. On the globe, the oldest objects are drawn in the warmest color. Here the globe shows only the objects in a thin slice through the Earth's center, with heights above the surface drawn 2.5 times their true scale, so the layers at different heights separate.

Payload reentries rose from 116 in 2020 to 1,111 in 2025

1,111 payloads reentered in 2025, and 671 of them were Starlink satellites, which had been in orbit for a median of 4.0 years when they came down. Counting every type, 1,905 objects reentered in 2025. Debris reentries peaked at 2,055 in 2022, the year after the Cosmos 1408 test.

Rocket bodies come down fastest: the median rocket body that has reentered did so 28 days after launch, since most upper stages are left in low orbits. While this section is on screen the globe replays January 2024 to today: the 5,123 objects with a cataloged orbit that reentered in that time are drawn in orange, and each one sinks into the atmosphere as its decay date passes.

411 objects left Earth orbit for the Moon, the Sun and the planets

The catalog also keeps the objects that escaped. 202 now circle the Sun, 109 of them rocket stages and 90 of them payloads. 102 went to the Moon, where 54 crashed, 11 landed and 37 went into orbit. 31 went to Mars and 29 to Venus, and five are on paths out of the solar system: Pioneer 10 and 11, Voyager 1 and 2, and one Falcon 9 upper stage.

The United States owns 240 of the 411 and Russia 88. The globe now shows the Moon at its true distance, about 60 Earth radii away. Scrolling on flies out to it: the objects that crashed or landed there are drawn on its surface, and those that went into orbit circle it. Point at one to see its catalog entry.

About the data

Source

The data is the satellite catalog (SATCAT) that CelesTrak publishes at celestrak.org/pub/satcat.csv, downloaded on September 23, 2026. CelesTrak builds it from the U.S. Space Force catalog released on Space-Track.org. Owner and launch site names come from CelesTrak's code tables, and the land shapes on the globe from Natural Earth.

What one row is

One row is one cataloged object: a payload, a rocket body, a piece of debris or an unidentified object. Each row carries the catalog number and international designator, the object type, owner, launch date and launch site, the decay date if the object has reentered, an operational status for payloads, and the latest orbit: period, inclination, apogee and perigee. The file has 70,745 rows and 17 columns, with launch dates from October 4, 1957 to September 21, 2026.

Rows left out

No rows are dropped from the counts. The altitude, inclination and age sections, and the globe, use only objects in Earth orbit with a cataloged orbit (34,500 of the 34,831 objects in Earth orbit). The globe also needs an inclination, which 4 geosynchronous satellites lack, so the globes on both pages draw 34,496. The 411 objects beyond Earth orbit appear only in their own section. The radar cross-section column is not used, because the catalog stopped filling it for objects launched after 2017.

When an object entered the catalog

A payload or rocket body enters the catalog on its launch date. A debris piece carries the launch date of the object it broke off, which can be decades before the breakup, and the payloads released from the space station carry the station's 1998 launch date. For these, and for the unidentified objects, the date is estimated from the catalog number, since numbers are handed out in order. Taking the payloads and rocket bodies in catalog-number order, the estimate is a rolling median of their launch dates over 51 neighbors, then a running maximum, so that the estimate never goes back in time as the numbers rise, then interpolated at each catalog number. An object enters on the later of its launch date and that estimate less 30 days, because new objects often receive their numbers some days after they are first tracked, and never after its reentry date.

An object counts as in Earth orbit on a date when it entered the catalog on or before that date and has not reentered by then. The yearly and monthly in-orbit counts, the timeline on the globe and the ages in the age section use these dates.

Definitions

  • In Earth orbit: no decay date, and an orbit centered on Earth (objects docked to the space station included).
  • Active payload: a payload with operational status of operational, partially operational, backup, spare or extended mission (codes +, P, B, S, X). Two rocket bodies also carry the code + and are not counted.
  • Starlink: a payload whose name starts with STARLINK. Two debris pieces with the name are not counted.
  • Mean altitude: the average of apogee and perigee, in km above the surface.
  • Near-circular orbit: eccentricity below 0.25, computed from apogee, perigee and the Earth's radius.
  • Russia (USSR): CelesTrak's owner code CIS, which covers the Soviet Union and Russia.
  • Median years in orbit: decay date minus launch date, for objects that have reentered.

Payloads released from the space station

The catalog gives the 416 small satellites released from the International Space Station the station's own launch date, November 20, 1998. In the yearly and decade counts of payloads they are counted in the year they entered the catalog instead, which is close to the year they were released. Every other object is counted in its launch year.

Rates and shares

Every percentage is a count divided by the count of the group named in the same sentence, for example Starlink active payloads divided by all active payloads. The owner shares divide each owner's payloads by all payloads launched in that decade. Medians are taken over the objects in the group. 2026 is a partial year: launches run through September 21 and reentries through September 23.

How the globe is drawn

Every object is drawn on an ellipse with its cataloged apogee, perigee and inclination, and moves at the speed that orbit implies, sped up 60 times. The catalog does not record which way each orbit's plane points or where the object is along it, so those two angles are assigned at random for each object. The one exception is Starlink: the satellites from one launch are drawn in one shared orbital plane, spaced evenly along it. The shells, bands and tilts on the globe are real; the position of any single object is not. Pointing at an object shows its catalog entry. In the altitude section heights are drawn on a square-root scale, and in the age section at 2.5 times their true scale.

On the timeline and in the breakup section, the pieces of each of the ten largest breakups start out together, burst outward and spread along their orbits over the following months. This shows how a debris cloud disperses, not where the pieces were. The points around the Moon are placed at random: those for objects that crashed or landed sit on its surface, the rest circle it.

Files

The raw catalog, the code tables and the scripts that turn them into this page are in the project repository, and prepare_data.py prints every number quoted above.
